title: Code Review & Engineering Standards
requirement: Conduct code reviews, establish engineering standards, enforce architectural best practices.

questions.question: What is the purpose of code review beyond catching bugs?
questions.answer: Catching bugs is the visible payoff, but the durable value is knowledge spread, so more than one person understands each subsystem. Review is also the cheapest architecture checkpoint, since drift shows in a diff long before an incident. If reviews only find typos, we're reviewing the wrong things.
questions.keyTakeaway: Review spreads knowledge, enforces design, and catches bugs, in that order of leverage.

questions.question: What is on your personal checklist when you review a pull request?
questions.answer: I read the description first and check that the intent matches the code. Then correctness, edge cases, tests and naming a newcomer can follow. Then structure: right layer, duplication, any contract other teams rely on. Style is the tools' job.
questions.keyTakeaway: Intent, correctness, tests, structure, naming; leave style to the tools.

questions.question: How do you give hard feedback in a review without making it personal?
questions.answer: I comment on the code and its consequences, not the author: this loop retries forever when the broker is down. I ask before giving verdicts, since the author may know what the diff doesn't show. I mark must-fix versus preference, and I praise good work.
questions.keyTakeaway: Critique the code and consequences, question before judging, label blocking versus preference.

diagram.title: Blocking or preference?
diagram.condition: Would you roll back the merge?

questions.question: How do you set standards for pull request size and review turnaround?
questions.answer: Big pull requests get skimmed, so I want small, single-purpose changes and a first review within one business day. Slow reviews push people onto long branches and bigger PRs. I track latency and size as team trends, never individual scores.
questions.keyTakeaway: Small PRs plus one-day first review; measure trends, and pre-walk through the unavoidable monsters.

questions.question: How do you enforce standards without turning reviews into a rule fight?
questions.answer: I automate every rule a machine can run: formatters, linters, type checks and pipeline gates. Humans review design fit, failure handling and whether the tests are honest. When review surfaces a new rule, I turn it into a lint rule. A manual rule has to earn its place through recurring incidents.
questions.keyTakeaway: Automate every enforceable rule; keep human review for judgment, and codify new rules on the spot.

questions.question: You and another senior disagree about a design inside a pull request. How is it resolved?
questions.answer: I move it out of the PR thread into a short design discussion. I write both positions down as options and judge them on delivery risk, operability and reversibility. Then a named decider, the area owner or an escalation path, makes the call, and I record it. I never let whoever merges first win.
questions.keyTakeaway: Promote the fight to a design decision with criteria and a decider; never merge-race a disagreement.

questions.question: How do you know your review culture is working?
questions.answer: I watch defect flow and knowledge spread, not review counts. Warning signs are escaped defects a review should have caught and PRs only one person can review. Healthy signs are comments shifting from bugs to design. I also ask whether authors feel helped or policed.
questions.keyTakeaway: Track escaped defects and single-reviewer risk; the comments should drift from bugs to design.

questions.question: How do you keep code reviews meaningful when the team is shipping under a hard deadline?
questions.answer: A deadline changes the scope of review, not its honesty. I ship a thinner slice instead of a shallower review. For urgent changes I rank by risk: correctness first, then blast radius, then data or security, then cosmetics. Structural comments go into a follow-up ticket due within a day or two. I refuse the rubber stamp, because a missed defect costs more than the delay.
questions.keyTakeaway: Ship a smaller diff instead of a shallower review, and give urgent merges a tracked follow-up pass.

steps.label: Follow-up ticket
steps.note: due in a day or two

questions.question: How do you keep reviews from drowning authors in nitpicks while still catching what actually matters?
questions.answer: Every comment spends the author's attention, so my test is whether I'd roll back the merge over it. If not, it's a suggestion. I keep blocking comments rare, otherwise authors dismiss them all. Repeated nits become tooling: the third missing null check becomes a lint rule, not a fourth comment.
questions.keyTakeaway: A blocking comment must carry roll-back severity; repeated nits graduate into tooling, not more comments.

diagram.title: Blocking or suggestion
diagram.condition: Would I roll back the merge over this comment?

questions.question: What do you expect to see in a pull request description, and what does not belong there?
questions.answer: I want what changed and why, how it was verified, and the risks, like a migration that runs or a flag whose default moved. Screenshots help for visual changes. I skip abandoned attempts and pasted ticket text. My test is whether someone could understand this diff from the description alone in six months.
questions.keyTakeaway: A description carries what, why, how it was verified, and risks; narrative history belongs in commits and docs.

questions.question: What do you look for when you review the tests in a pull request specifically?
questions.answer: I read the tests before the implementation, since they're the spec. First, honesty: would any fail if the feature broke, or is it so mocked it only verifies the mock? Second, edge cases and error paths, with specific assertions. Third, brittleness like sleeps. I also watch for tests bent to pass, like an expectation loosened to match buggy output.
questions.keyTakeaway: Read the tests first: they must fail when the feature breaks, cover error paths, and never be bent to pass.

questions.question: What is your own routine before you ask someone to review your pull request?
questions.answer: I review my own diff first, top to bottom in the review UI, which clears out debug lines and half-finished renames. I write the description before the final read, since explaining exposes gaps. CI is green before I ping anyone. I pick the reviewer who owns the risky area, not whoever approves fastest.
questions.keyTakeaway: Read your own diff as a reviewer would, annotate the non-obvious, and route to the owner, not the fastest approver.

questions.question: A review has bounced back and forth five times with no convergence. What do you do?
questions.answer: Five rounds means the medium has failed. I stop the line comments and get on a call with the diff shared, because that settles in two minutes what comments drag across three days. Then I address every point in one push. Afterwards I ask why it happened. If standards surfaced one per round, I write them down.
questions.keyTakeaway: After several stale rounds, walk the diff together and converge in one consolidated push; write down any newly surfaced standard.

questions.question: How do you use code review to bring a junior engineer up without becoming their bottleneck?
questions.answer: Review is a team's highest-frequency coaching moment. Early on my comments explain instead of judge: the why, an example, what good looks like, because a verdict without a reason teaches compliance, not judgment. Then I taper off, so verdicts become questions and my attention shifts from syntax to design. I never rubber-stamp their work.
questions.keyTakeaway: Coach with explained comments, taper guidance as judgment grows, and pair on juniors' first reviews of others.

questions.question: How does your review change when a pull request touches security-sensitive code?
questions.answer: Security review is tracing attacker-controlled data. I follow untrusted input from entry to every sink, like a query, shell call or redirect, and validate or parameterize at the boundary. I check authorization at each layer, because bugs usually live below the careful-looking controller. I want a test showing an unauthenticated request gets 403, and a second reviewer on high-stakes changes.
questions.keyTakeaway: Trace untrusted input to every sink, check authorization per layer, and require tests that prove the check.

questions.question: Production is down and someone wants to push a fix straight to main. How should emergency reviews work?
questions.answer: An incident suspends ceremony, not accountability. The fix can merge before review, but the bypass is loud: a hotfix tag, a note in the incident channel and a named revert plan. During the fire, review narrows to blast radius and rollback. Afterwards the diff gets a real review within days. I write the emergency path down in advance.
questions.keyTakeaway: Merge first only during an active incident, with a visible bypass and a full review once the fire is out.

questions.question: How do you review a pull request in a subsystem you know almost nothing about?
questions.answer: I say up front that I'm unfamiliar with the area, because faking confidence gives the author false assurance. Outsider questions often find real bugs. I review what transfers: does the diff match its description, are failures handled, does it follow surrounding patterns. For high-stakes changes I add the domain owner. Mine covers structure, theirs covers truth.
questions.keyTakeaway: Declare your unfamiliarity, review what transfers, and recruit a domain owner for high-stakes calls.

questions.question: What is your honest take on AI-assisted code review tools, and how do you slot them into the process?
questions.answer: AI reviewers are a tireless first pass, never an authority. They're good at the mechanical layer, like null paths, missing validation and leaked secrets, but they don't know the product, and they state hallucinated criticisms as confidently as real ones. So the bot runs on every PR and is non-blocking. Humans own intent and design, and accountability stays with whoever merges.
questions.keyTakeaway: AI reviewers are a tireless non-blocking first pass; judgment and merge accountability stay with humans.

questions.question: How do you keep review turnaround sane when authors and reviewers sit in different time zones?
questions.answer: It's routing, not heroics. An ownership map guarantees every subsystem a qualified reviewer who's awake within a few hours of any author. Descriptions are complete enough to work with the author asleep, and comments are written as decisions with reasons. Escalation is automatic: no first review in a business day goes to the team channel, and two days goes to leads.
questions.keyTakeaway: Follow-the-sun coverage, self-sufficient descriptions, and automatic escalation beat any single-region turnaround promise.

questions.question: When do you skip the pull request cycle and pair on the code instead?
questions.answer: I skip the PR cycle when the value is deep knowledge transfer, which PRs deliver poorly: exploratory spikes where most code gets thrown away, a subsystem with one maintainer, sensitive work like credential handling, and reviews that looped three times. Pairing replaces the conversation, never the verification. We still write tests and use the same pipeline gates.
questions.keyTakeaway: Pair when work is exploratory, sensitive, or single-maintainer; pairing replaces the conversation, never the verification.

questions.question: How do you review a pull request that is thousands of lines of generated or mechanically migrated code?
questions.answer: Nobody reviews three thousand generated lines, so I review the generator. A migration script or codegen template gets full scrutiny, because every output line inherits its bugs. I check it's deterministic and safe to rerun, audit a stratified sample including the gnarliest files, and cover the bulk with the full suite or an empty behavioral diff. Generated code gets its own commit.
questions.keyTakeaway: Review the generator and a stratified sample, verify the bulk mechanically, and isolate generated code from future diffs.

steps.label: Isolate the blob
steps.note: own commit, no blame or formatting

questions.question: What is your strategy for reviewing a large refactor without rubber-stamping it or stalling it for weeks?
questions.answer: A refactor as one giant diff gets approved unread. I insist on a sequence: extract helpers with identical behavior, then a mechanical rename, then any behavior change in its own diff, each landing green. The author proves preservation with characterization tests written before the refactor. I review mechanical steps with search, not eyes, and spend my judgment on the new seams.
questions.keyTakeaway: Sequence a refactor into behavior-preserving steps, demand proof of equivalence, and spend judgment on the new seams.

questions.question: An author and a reviewer have deadlocked and neither will budge. What is the escalation path?
questions.answer: A deadlock needs a standing rule, written before anyone is angry. The PR waits and doesn't merge. After a business day, a named decider like the tech lead gets a written request with both options, the criteria each serves and the cost of delay. Escalation is the process working, not one side winning. I police silent resolution hardest, like the midnight force-push.
questions.keyTakeaway: Deadlocks get a standing rule: time-box, then a written decision request to a named owner; silent merges erode the process.

questions.question: How do you handle review when a change cuts across code owned by several teams?
questions.answer: It works when ownership is declared before the PR opens, in a CODEOWNERS file. Each owner approves their own slice, and one broad approval never covers someone else's contract. A bot-enforced rule beats a polite norm. If an owner is slow, I ship an adapter facade in my own code, not a drive-by edit in theirs.
questions.keyTakeaway: Declare ownership in CODEOWNERS, require each owner's approval on their slice, and adapt around slow owners.

questions.question: How do you review a change in legacy code that has no meaningful test coverage?
questions.answer: In legacy code the risk is unreviewed behavior, so I first ask the author how they know nothing broke. If they can't say, I ask for characterization tests that pin the current output, even where it's wrong. I keep the fix minimal and separate from cleanup, so each can revert alone, and I name the residual risk honestly.
questions.keyTakeaway: Pin existing behavior with characterization tests first, separate cleanup from fixes, and state residual risk honestly.
